_comment: Per-town data for build_town_pages.py. RULE: only verified facts go in here. 'official_url' must return HTTP 200 and must be the town's own domain — never a deep link that is likely to rot. Leave a field null rather than guessing; the template omits null fields entirely. 'energy_code' is only filled where the town's own building department publishes it.
_verified: 2026-08-08 — official_url values checked with curl (200 unless noted); Norwood facts read from the town's own Building Department document list.

towns.name: Norwood
towns.energy_code: Norwood has opted into the Specialized (opt-in) Stretch Energy Code. The Building Department publishes both a residential opt-in stretch code document and an opt-in stretch code permitting checklist, and an ADU has to be designed to that standard.
local_notes: The Building Department's own ADU reference is the state regulation itself — 760 CMR 71.00, Protected Use Accessory Dwelling Units — so Norwood is applying the state framework directly rather than a separate local ADU bylaw.
Norwood publishes a "Plot Plan Required" document. Expect to supply a plot plan with the permit application, which is also the first thing we ask for.
towns._project_images_note: Files must exist at images/norwood/<file> or the gallery is omitted entirely — the generator checks, so a missing file can never ship as a broken image. 'lead' is the single photo used on the homepage built-work block. Kept deliberately short: five photos that each do distinct work, rather than the full listing set, most of which was near-duplicate empty rooms.

towns.name: Newton
local_notes: Newton has a number of local historic districts. The state ADU law lets municipalities apply stricter design standards inside a historic district, so confirm whether your parcel sits in one before committing to an exterior direction.

towns.name: Brookline
local_notes: Brookline lots are frequently tight, and the state ADU law does not waive local setback or height limits. Buildable-area review matters more here than the 900 sf cap does.

towns.name: Cambridge
local_notes: Much of Cambridge is zoned for two- and three-family use rather than single-family. The state by-right ADU provision is keyed to single-family zoning, so which district your parcel sits in determines whether the by-right path applies at all.

towns.name: Somerville
local_notes: Somerville is dense and largely multi-family zoned, and it is well served by transit — which matters, because no parking space can be required for an ADU within a half mile of a transit stop.

towns.name: Boston
towns.official_label: Accessory Dwelling Units in Boston — City of Boston
local_notes: Boston runs its own ADU process rather than the statewide by-right provision, and the city's program is aimed at owners of 1-, 2-, and 3-family homes who live at the property.

The city distinguishes internal ADUs (basement or attic conversions) from external ones (an attached addition or a detached backyard structure). Which one you're doing changes the drawing set substantially.
Some Boston projects still require Zoning Board of Appeal review before a building permit is issued, so the timeline here is less predictable than in a by-right town.

Boston offers things most towns don't: a published ADU guidebook, free monthly design and budget workshops, and a financial assistance program for income-eligible homeowners. Worth using before you pay anyone, including us.
